title: Treat Him as an Unbeliever: Church Discipline and Excommunication
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro
summary: This sermon examines the biblical basis and practice of church discipline, particularly excommunication, as taught in Matthew 18 and 1 Corinthians 5. Pastor Lyro clarifies what excommunication is, how it should be administered, and how church members should relate to those who have been excommunicated, emphasizing that discipline is ultimately an act of love aimed at repentance and restoration.

outline.title: What is Church Discipline?
subpoints: Church discipline is a God-ordained authoritative process to keep Christ's body pure and bring unrepentant members to repentance
It may culminate in a declaration that a person is not a brother, with hope for repentance and reconciliation
Matthew 18 shows the shepherd pursuing the lost sheep, representing the church pursuing the wandering member
Both Matthew 18 (reconciliation) and 1 Corinthians 5 (purity) are essential aspects of biblical discipline

outline.title: How is Church Discipline Conducted?
subpoints: Through faithful preaching of God's Word by the Holy Spirit
Preventively through practicing the 'one another' commands in Scripture
Through pastoral counseling
According to Matthew 18's escalating process: private conversation, then with witnesses, then before the church
The scope of involvement must match the scope of the sin

outline.title: What is Excommunication?
subpoints: The word means 'out of communion'—placed outside the visible church
Demonstrated by removal of access to the Lord's Supper
A declaration that impenitence reveals unbelief
Christians live repentant lives; refusal to repent shows oneself to be an unbeliever
Excommunication declares a person in a dangerous place outside Christ's protection
It is turning someone over to Satan in hope of working repentance

outline.title: How Should We Relate to the Excommunicated?
subpoints: Excommunication should produce mourning in the church and self-examination
Treat them as unbelievers, but as Jesus treated tax collectors and foreigners—with evangelistic compassion
Do not avoid or hide from them; instead, seek them out to preach the gospel
Call them to repentance, share Scripture, pray for them
Family relationships continue; separation applies only to participation in church life and fellowship
Romans 16:17-18, 1 Corinthians 5:11-13, and 2 Thessalonians 3:6 address different issues and do not prohibit evangelistic engagement

outline.title: Why Address This One Person When Others Sin Too?
subpoints: God graciously makes certain sins known so the church can exercise its responsibility
Many disciplinary cases end in private repentance, unseen by the congregation
All things are known to God; hidden sins will eventually be revealed
Addressing this case publicly addresses all unrepentant sinners in the church

outline.title: Application: Three-Fold Impact
subpoints: To the unrepentant: Christ still calls you; your only hope is in Him; His mercy is greater than all sin
To believers: Pursue holiness, confess sin quickly, receive correction gratefully, examine yourselves; church discipline should produce humility, not pride
To the church: Love sinners enough to tell them truth; real love weeps, warns, prays, pursues, and never stops longing for restoration
Be a church both holy and compassionate, unwilling to compromise Christ's honor or give up on wanderers

outline.title: The Grace of God Underlying Discipline
subpoints: Church discipline demonstrates Christ's love for His people and His church
It is an instrument of the good shepherd seeking the one who has wandered
We all deserve to be cut off from God's kingdom; we stand only because Jesus was cut off for us
The door of mercy remains open as long as God grants life
All whom the Father has given to Christ will come to Him and will not be cast out

transcript:
## Scripture Reading

> "What do you think if a man has a hundred sheep and one of them goes astray? Does he not leave the ninety-nine and go to the mountains to seek the one that has strayed? And if he should find it, I assure you, he rejoices more over that sheep than over the ninety-nine that did not go astray. Even so, it is not the will of your Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish. Moreover, if your brother sins against you, go and tell him his fault between you and him alone. If he hears you, you have gained your brother. But if he will not hear, take with you one or two more, that by the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established. And if he refuses to hear them, tell it to the church. But if he refuses even to hear the church, let him be to you like a heathen and a tax collector. Assuredly, I say to you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven. And whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven. Again, I say to you that if two of you agree on earth concerning anything that they ask, it will be done for them by my Father in heaven. For where two or three are gathered together in my name, I am there in the midst of them." (Matthew 18:12-20)

## Introduction

Our God works all things for the good of those who love Him and are called according to His purposes. Even when we think the thing being worked out is excommunication. If nothing else, what we are doing here today gives us the opportunity to consider God's grace even in the worst thing—the worst thing that could ever be said about a person—that he is outside of the love of Christ.

When one thinks of excommunication in the American context, one's mind might quickly go to Nathaniel Hawthorne's *Scarlet Letter*. Images of Hester Prynne with a red letter A embroidered on her dress tend to form in our minds, and feelings of indignation flood into our thinking as we think of the injustice of it all—where Hester has to wear the Scarlet Letter while the minister who committed adultery with her cowardly hides in his study.

One also tends to think that Hawthorne accurately describes what excommunication is and how one is to relate to the person who has been excommunicated. And though it provides a glimpse into the human heart, the *Scarlet Letter* is not a handbook for church discipline.

My desire this morning is to answer several questions regarding church discipline, especially what excommunication is and how we should relate to one who has been excommunicated. But my ultimate goal is for us to behold Christ this morning, because there is no one more beautiful and better for us to behold on His day.

## What Is Church Discipline?

The first question I want to answer is: What is church discipline?

Here is a succinct definition. In our Constitution we have a whole document of several chapters describing church discipline. I am going to try summarizing to one paragraph: Church discipline is a God-ordained authoritative process to keep Christ's body pure and bring unrepentant members to repentance. The process may culminate with a declaration that a person whom we thought was a brother is not a brother, all in the hope of repentance and reconciliation.

Matthew 18 focuses on the repentance and reconciliation aspect of it. Notice in the context leading to verse 15 in the passages that we read that we have the shepherd in verses 12 and 13 who goes after the lost sheep. The shepherd abandons everything he has to go after this one lost sheep to bring that sheep back into the fold, into the fellowship of the church. In a sense, brothers and sisters, when we do church discipline appropriately, when the whole church pursues church discipline, it is the shepherd and the ninety-nine sheep pursuing that one lost sheep and bringing him back into the fold.

Peter understood that when Jesus finished talking about this process in verses 15 through 18, the main gist of what Christ was teaching was reconciliation and restoration. We see that by the question he asks in verse 21: "Lord, how many times should he forgive?" Peter understood that Jesus was getting to forgiveness. Peter thought he was being very magnanimous, very gracious by being willing to forgive seven times. But we know what our Lord says in verse 22: "No, seventy times seven, or as many times as is necessary." And then He gives a parable in the following verses about a man who owed a great debt, was forgiven by the king, but then refused to forgive another man.

Matthew 18 is not the only passage that talks about church discipline. There are others, including 1 Corinthians chapter 5, in which Paul focuses on the purity of the body of Christ. So repentance and purity go hand in hand in church discipline.

In 1 Corinthians 5, verses 6 and 7, Paul says:

> "Your glorying is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump? Therefore purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new lump since you truly are unleavened. For indeed Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed for us." (1 Corinthians 5:6-7)

Then in verse 11, Paul says:

> "But now I have written to you not to keep company with anyone named a brother who is sexually immoral or covetous or an idolater or a reviler or a drunkard or an extortioner—not even to eat with such a person." (1 Corinthians 5:11)

And then in verse 13, Paul says:

> "But those who are outside God judges. Therefore put away from yourselves the evil person." (1 Corinthians 5:13)

Brothers and sisters, the church is the bride of Christ, the body of Christ, the temple of Christ. To allow one who is unrepentant to be identified with that body is to say that Christ himself is sinful.

In both aspects of church discipline, it may lead to a declaration that the one whom we thought was a brother is not a brother. We see that in Matthew 18, verse 17, when the Lord Jesus says:

> "Let him be to you like a heathen and a tax collector." (Matthew 18:17)

Now it is important for us to understand that church discipline does not cause anything. There is no effectual power in church discipline. In declaring somebody to be excommunicated, that is all we are doing—we are declaring that. All that church discipline does is match what the Bible says with what somebody is saying or doing, and then declare what the Bible says concerning that thing—that that person is either saying or doing.

But it is an authoritative process. The final proclamation in Matthew 18:17 is a command. "Let him be" is not a choice that we have; it is something that we must obey if we want to obey the Lord Jesus Christ. And when done according to the Scriptures, it is a declaration of what has happened in heaven.

In verse 18, Jesus says:

> "Assuredly, I say to you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven." (Matthew 18:18)

I am not sure why translations keep this translation when the language behind it is so obviously different. The way it is written here gives the impression that what you do here causes something to happen in heaven. But literally, what Jesus says is that what you do on earth will have been done in heaven. The Greek is a future periphastic perfect. What we are doing here is declaring what God says, what heaven has done. But it is done in the authority of Christ.

In 1 Corinthians 5, verses 4 and 5, Paul says:

> "In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you are gathered together, along with my spirit, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus." (1 Corinthians 5:4-5)

Some of you might wonder why do this publicly? Because that is what Paul tells us to do. That is what the Holy Spirit tells us. When you are gathered together, along with Paul's spirit, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, you deliver such one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.

## How Is Discipline to Be Done?

So that is the first question: What is church discipline? The second is: How is discipline to be done?

First, through the preaching of the Word of God. By God's grace, many difficulties are quietly prevented. The Spirit works mightily through the preaching of the Word, even before problems arise, because the Holy Spirit blesses the faithful proclamation of His Word.

Church discipline is also done preventively by the practicing of the "one another" commands in the Bible. And perhaps we fail in that way. How many of us have gone to a brother and said, "Brother, what is going on? Brother, we missed you. Brother, where have you been? Brother, let us get together."

Thirdly, counseling is another way that church discipline is conducted, but in a preventive way.

Matthew 18 gives us the outline of what to do when willful sins have been committed. The initial scope of involvement in verse 15 must be equivalent to the scope of the sin. Whatever, if the sin was private, you deal with it that way. If it is public, you deal with it that way as well.

If the brother or sister continues to be unrepentant, the scope of the involvement increases. Bring a couple of people and continue to talk to the brother. If there is no turning away from the sin, then the church through its representatives starts an official disciplinary process that we have at the beginning of verse 17. And if the person remains incorrigible—that is, there is no repentance—then the church is to excommunicate him.

## What Is Excommunication?

So what is church discipline? How is it to be done? And then the third question I want to ask is: What is excommunication?

The word itself means "out of communion." It means to be placed outside of the communion of the visible church, and that is demonstrated by not having access to the Lord's Supper.

In Matthew 18, verse 17, Christ defines excommunication as being like a foreigner or a heathen and a tax collector. These were two categories of people who were outside the covenant people of God. They were unbelievers. Therefore, to excommunicate someone is to declare that his impenitence—his lack of repentance—through that he has shown himself to be an unbeliever.

Brothers and sisters, friends, the Christian does not live a perfect life. If that was the case, there would be only one Christian in history, and that would be the Lord Jesus Christ. But a Christian lives a repentant life. Repentance is not just what begins the Christian life, but is what keeps us connected to Christ. We are not free from sin. If my heart was displayed on the screen here, you would be horrified. I tend to think that if any of our hearts was displayed on the screen here, we would be horrified. And yet we are not called to perfection. God already has the perfect one. His name is Jesus Christ. He does not need us to be perfect, but He needs us to repent. He calls us to repent. And when a person refuses to repent, by his own impenitence, he has shown himself to be an unbeliever.

In 1 Corinthians 5:5, Paul defines excommunication as turning the person over to Satan in hopes that this will work repentance in him. Paul says in verse 5:

> "Deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus." (1 Corinthians 5:5)

So excommunication declares a person to be in a very dangerous place—outside of Christ, outside of fellowship with believers, unable to feed on Christ at the Lord's Supper, outside of the promises of the New Covenant. The point that the Holy Spirit says in Hebrews 10:31:

> "It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God." (Hebrews 10:31)

Wilhelmus Abracal was a Dutch pastor in the eighteenth century. He wrote a super helpful book—I encourage you to read it. It is four volumes, but you should not be scared of it. He says to excommunicate a person is to deprive him of Christ's protection and to deliver such a person to him who rules beyond the boundaries of the church—that is, Satan.

So what is it? What is church discipline? How is it to be done? What is excommunication? And fourthly, how do we relate to a person who has been excommunicated?

## How to Relate to the Excommunicated

### The Church Should Mourn

First, the excommunication of a member of the church should cause mourning in the church. Paul says in 1 Corinthians 5:2:

> "You are puffed up and have not rather mourned that he who has done this deed might be taken away from among you." (1 Corinthians 5:2)

The mourning should cause the church to search its own corporate conscience to see whether part of the fault lies at its own feet. Brothers, where did we fail? How did we fail? And I urge us to consider that and examine our hearts that we might repent and not allow that to happen again.

Brothers and sisters, we should never have the attitude of "good riddance" when someone is removed from our midst. We must have the same attitude as the Father did in anxiously waiting for the prodigal son to come back. There did not take much convincing, did it, for the Father to receive the prodigal son back. That is where we need to be.

### Treat Them as Unbelievers, but with Gospel Compassion

But we relate to him as we would relate to an unbeliever who has made a mockery of the name of Christ by pretending to be a believer. And that is what Jesus means at the end of verse 17:

> "Let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector." (Matthew 18:17)

Heathen and tax collectors were not looked upon by the audience of Jesus' time as people who were fun to hang out with. As a matter of fact, they were socially avoided.

But Jesus seasons this understanding with the way he treated foreigners and tax collectors. Have you ever worked your way through the gospels and seen how did Jesus relate to heathens and to tax collectors? He evangelized them. They were the object of his evangelism, not necessarily of his fellowship. The compassion that was shown to them was the presentation of the gospel, not hanging out with them.

Even in Matthew 9, verses 10 through 13, where Jesus is having dinner with the tax collectors and the heathens and the Pharisees complain about it, do you remember what Jesus says he is doing? He says:

> "It is not the righteous but sinners that need repentance." (Matthew 9:10-13)

And he is preaching the gospel even to the heathen and to the tax collector.

To be exhorted to treat someone like an unbeliever seems to be so benign to us. It seems like, what is the difference? What is the power of it? How does it look like? What is the big deal? And the reason for that is that we often think this way because we treat the world as if it were the church and often we treat the church as if it were the world. We are more patient, more loving, more caring toward the world than we are toward the church. We enjoy more the company of unbelievers than we enjoy the company of believers.

And when you address that, people often say, "Oh, I am just trying to be salt and light to the world." Brothers and sisters, the saltiest salt and the brightest light are found in loving the brethren, not the world. If we really knew what it means to love the brethren, the command to treat them as not a brother would really shake us in our boots. We do not want that.

### What Does This Look Like in Real Life?

So how does it look like in real life? Do I have to avoid him? Do I run when I see him? And the answer is, kind of, and yes.

Again, Abracal says: If opportunity is there, or if in some edifying manner we can create an opportunity, then while manifesting the distance and separation between us and him, we must lament his wretched condition and exhort him to repentance.

Do not avoid the one who has been excommunicated. Preach the gospel. Preach the gospel. And do not buy into the foolishness that you are going to preach the gospel and if necessary use words. You cannot do that. Either use words or you are not preaching the gospel.

Call up Nathaniel. He may not answer. He has not been answering our calls. Go to where he is. Reach out to him. Talk to him. Share the Scriptures with him. Remember the parable of the unrighteous judge: the widow came and knocked so many times at his door that he eventually said, "All right already, I will do what you want." Can Nathaniel say that of us? Or if we call him this week, he might say, "Wow, you have never talked to me before, or it has been years since I heard from you."

### Regarding Family Relationships

Regarding family relationships, Francis Turretin (I like quoting dead guys because we already know all the mistakes they made and we do not have to wonder about something happening in the future) said this: "Excommunication cannot sever the natural and moral bonds by which men are mutually held together. Rather, this separation ought to be extended only to those parts of intercourse which would seem to imply involvement in and approval of sin."

So we are going to be seeking this person out, not to hang out, but to call him to repentance. And we want them in church because we want them to be in church. We want them to hear the Word of the Lord.

### Addressing Common Passages

Now, how about those passages? So I am telling you, do not avoid the excommunicated. There used to be a church that we were familiar with that would tell their people, "If you see them in the supermarket, run away." Literally, that was destruction. "If they are on the aisle, do not go to that aisle." I am not telling you to do that. I want you to engage the excommunicated. I want you to talk to them. I want you to go and tell them, "I miss you. Friend, I am so sad I cannot call you brother, but I want you to repent. Come with me."

But how about all those passages that say that we are not supposed to have anything to do with those that are excommunicated? Well, I do not think those exist. At least if you interpret them correctly. There are three of them that people bring up.

One is Romans 16, verses 17 and 18, where Paul says:

> "Now I urge you, brethren, note those who cause divisions and offenses contrary to the doctrine which you learned and avoid them." (Romans 16:17-18)

Well, this passage deals with false teachers who are actively teaching another gospel. We are to avoid them. We are not to credit them. We are to discredit them. We are to engage what they are saying so that they will not keep on teaching it.

Another passage is 1 Corinthians 5, verses 11 through 13, where it says:

> "But now I have written to you not to keep company with anyone named a brother who is sexually immoral or covetous or an idolater or a reviler or a drunkard or an extortioner—not even to eat with such a person. But those who are outside God judges. Therefore put away from yourselves the evil person." (1 Corinthians 5:11-13)

I want you to notice that this is spoken to the church. If you read it, you see all kinds of plurals there. It is not talking to an individual here, but to the church as a whole. The church has declared this person outside its boundary. The church is to make sure that it is understood by all that this person who claims to be a brother is not a brother at all. The taking of leaven out is making sure that everybody in the church and outside knows that what this individual is doing cannot be done in the name of Christ. And when the church does that, it removes the confusion or the leavening effects of the sin.

The church is not to participate with this person in the one meal that the Lord Jesus Christ has given to it: the Lord's Supper. That is the exhortation not to eat with them. This is not a prohibition to have dinner with the person. This is saying that the person may not participate in the Lord's Supper simply because they denied the Lord part of it.

The third passage is 2 Thessalonians 3, verses 6 and 15. I am just going to read a couple of verses of that passage. This is what Paul says:

> "But we commend you, brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ that you withdraw from every brother who walks disorderly and not according to the tradition which he received from us... Yet do not count him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother." (2 Thessalonians 3:6, 15)

Whatever else this passage means, it is not talking about excommunication. And the reason I know that is because it urges the church to treat this person as a brother, not as an unbeliever, but as a brother. So whatever Paul is urging here, it does not apply to this area.

And I know that some of these answers may be generating more questions. I am happy to talk to anybody who wants to talk to me. You just have to find me. I will be available.

## Why Address One Person?

Now, the last question I want to answer is this: Why are you picking on this one person? That is what you might think. Why are you picking on Nathaniel? How about all the other sinners in this church? Why are you not addressing them?

Well, literally, that is what I am doing right now—addressing us, the other sinners in the church.

Another thing is that there are a lot of disciplined cases that end before they become public because God grants repentance to the center and you do not need to know about it. And I am sure that there are people among us living lives that dishonor God and that warrant church discipline, but we do not know about it.

Brothers and sisters, it is a gracious act of God when he makes sure that one's sins find him out so that Christ's church can do the one thing that God promises to bless.

And if you are thinking that you are super smart because you have been able to hide your sins, I warn you that all things are open and bare before Him with whom you have to do. What we have done here this morning should impact us in at least three ways.

## Three-Fold Application

### To the One in Unrepentant Sin

To the one living in unrepentant sin among us, Christ still calls you to himself. If you recognize yourself in the person described here today, do not harden your heart. The purpose of discipline is not to convince you that there is no hope. It is to show you that your only hope is Christ.

The same Savior who welcomed tax collectors and sinners still receives everyone who comes to him in repentance and faith. No sin is greater than his mercy for those who turn to him.

If you are an unbeliever among us, it does not really matter what sin you have committed. Christ's grace is greater than the sum of all your sins.

### To Believers

To the believer, brothers and sisters, let this drive us to humility and watchfulness. Church discipline should never produce pride. The question is not "How could he do such a thing?" but rather "Apart from the grace of God, where would I be?"

We stand only because Christ upholds us. So pursue holiness. Confess sin, and do that quickly. Receive loving correction gratefully, and bear one another's burdens before sin hardens the heart.

As Paul says:

> "Let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed, lest he fall." (1 Corinthians 10:12)

### To the Church

And to the church, love the wandering enough to tell them the truth. The world often defines love as affirmation—"Whatever you want." Christ defines love as pursuing sinners with the truth that leads to life.

Refusing to confront destructive sin is not mercy; it is indifference. If you are hiding behind the mercy excuse, you are doing something worse than hating the person. You are indifferent to the soul, to the destiny of the soul of that person.

Real love weeps. Real love warns. Real love prays. Real love pursues. And real love never stops longing for restoration.

Let us therefore be a church that is both holy and compassionate, unwilling to compromise Christ's honor, and unwilling to give up on those who wander from him.

As I said earlier, like the Father of the prodigal son, may we watch, may we pray, and may we eagerly wait the day when God grants repentance and brings the wandering sinner home.

## The Grace Underlying Discipline

Church discipline is one of the hardest responsibilities Christ has entrusted to his church. Yet it is also one of the clearest demonstrations that he loves his people.

Hebrews tells us that the Lord disciplines those whom he loves. When the church exercises discipline according to Christ's Word, it is not acting in anger or self-righteousness, but as an instrument of the good shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to seek the one who has wandered.

Brothers and sisters, today none of us should leave here thinking about somebody else's sin. We should leave here examining our own hearts. Everyone of us deserves to be outside of the kingdom of God. Everyone of us deserves to be cut off from the fellowship of God's people.

If we stand within Christ's church today, it is not because we have been more faithful than another, but because Jesus Christ was cut off for us. On the cross, He endured the curse, bore the wrath of God, and was forsaken so that all who repent and believe would never be cast away.

So let us guard our hearts against the deceitfulness of sin, and let us rejoice that the door of mercy remains open. As long as God grants life, the gospel continues to call sinners to repentance, and Christ continues to receive all who come to him in faith. All that the Father has given to him will come to him, and he will not cast them out.
